title: Science and technology
subtitle: cloning, ergonomics, insert, utilise, rotate
summary: Name the newer branches of science and use the formal verbs that scientists and technicians use every day.

lesson.heading: Traditional and new sciences
lesson.text: You probably know the traditional branches of science: **chemistry**, **physics**, **botany** and **zoology**. A number of fields have been established much more recently, and each one has its own name and its own vocabulary.

examples.text: She studied **botany** at university and now works in **genetic engineering**.
**Stem cell research** is one of the most promising fields in medicine.

lesson.heading: New sciences and what they study
rows: works with the genetic material (DNA) of living things to alter features; GM (genetically modified) foods are grown in some parts of the world
studies the design of physical working spaces and how people interact with them
studies the structure and function of the molecules associated with living things
enables machines to interpret speech, e.g. voice-to-text software
studies the use of human cells to treat diseases and injury and to repair the body
the creation of exact copies of plants or animals with the same genes as the originals
the science of growing plants without using soil

lesson.heading: Useful words from those definitions
rows: the way the parts of a system are organised
a basic chemical unit, a group of atoms
the smallest basic part of a plant or animal
making something new that did not exist before
the top layer of the earth's surface, in which plants grow

lesson.heading: Everyday technology
rows: a phone that also takes videos, runs apps and goes online
something like a laptop with a touch screen, for films and ebooks
a television you watch with special glasses for a realistic effect
a video camera that produces really sharp movies
satellite navigation, so you never lose your way
a screen that shows your photos any time you want

lesson.heading: Verbs in the laboratory
lesson.text: Note the collocations. To **experiment with** something is to try it out; **utilise** is a formal word for use. Lights **flash**, wheels **rotate** (turn), and you pull a **lever** - a bar or handle that controls a machine.

examples.text: He **experimented with** different materials before **utilising** the most suitable one.
The technician pressed a button and lights started **flashing**.
When she pulled the large **lever**, the wheel began to **rotate**.

lesson.heading: More scientific verbs
lesson.text: To **dissect** is to cut open a dead body or plant to study its parts; to **extract** is to take out. Chemicals **react** with each other when **combined**. After **analysing** a problem you **conclude** something, and a **flaw** is a fault, mistake or weakness.

examples.text: The zoologist **dissected** the animal and **extracted** its organs.
When they were **combined**, the two chemicals **reacted** violently with each other.
After **analysing** the problem, she **concluded** that there was a **flaw** in the theory.
**Insert** the disk into the DVD drive to **install** the software, or visit the website to download it.
examples.note: insert = put in; install = make ready to use

lesson.text: *Utilise*, *insert*, *extract* and *rotate* are the formal technical twins of *use*, *put in*, *take out* and *turn*. Use them in a report, not in conversation.

exercises.prompt: Match each scientist's description with the field they work in.

pairs.left: We grow the plants in liquids, without using soil.
The software interprets your speech and turns it into text.
We study workplaces and how people interact with them.
We make an exact copy of an animal with the same genes.
We study how human cells can repair the body.
I study the structure of the molecules in living organisms.

exercises.prompt: Many people refuse to eat genetically ___ foods. They consider GM foods to be unnatural.
exercises.explanation: GM stands for genetically modified: the field is genetic engineering.

exercises.prompt: By manipulating DNA, we can ___ hereditary features.
exercises.explanation: Alter means change, usually slightly. This is genetic engineering.

exercises.prompt: We're interested in workplaces and how people ___ with their working environment.
exercises.explanation: Interact with means communicate with or react to. The field is ergonomics.

exercises.prompt: 'I keep losing my way and I'm not good at reading maps.' What does this person need?
exercises.explanation: A satnav (satellite navigation, or GPS) tells you where to go.

exercises.prompt: 'My old camcorder doesn't produce really sharp movies.' What does this person need?
exercises.explanation: High-definition (HD) equipment produces a much sharper picture.

exercises.prompt: 'I want something like a laptop with a touch screen that I can watch films on or read ebooks.' What does this person need?
exercises.explanation: A tablet is a flat computer with a touch screen.

exercises.prompt: Match each sentence beginning with its ending.

pairs.right: that lever, it starts the machine.
that button, it turns the printer on.

pairs.left: I believe there is a flaw

exercises.prompt: The wheel began to ___ very quickly.
exercises.explanation: Rotate is the formal technical word for turn.

exercises.prompt: ___ the disk to install the software.
exercises.explanation: Insert is the formal technical word for put in; install means make ready to use.
Utilise is the formal technical word for use.

exercises.statement: We analysed the problem and concluded that it was a computer virus.
exercises.explanation: Correct. You analyse a problem and then conclude something from your analysis.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to describe a chemistry experiment.
exercises.answer: When they were combined, the two chemicals reacted violently with each other.
exercises.explanation: You combine chemicals, and they react with each other.
